Generalized Wishart measurement model for squared distances

Source: R/generalized_wishart.R
generalized_wishart.Rd

A function of class "terradish_measurement_model" that evaluates the generalized Wishart likelihood for an admissible pairwise genetic squared-distance matrix. This model requires a distance representation that is coherently related to a centered positive semidefinite covariance matrix; it is not valid for an arbitrary dissimilarity matrix. The effective marker degrees of freedom must also be supplied. For covariance-matrix data, use wishart_covariance.

Usage

generalized_wishart(
  E,
  S,
  phi,
  nu,
  gradient = TRUE,
  hessian = TRUE,
  partial = TRUE,
  nonnegative = TRUE,
  validate = FALSE
)

Arguments

E

Conductance-implied covariance matrix: the generalized inverse of the graph Laplacian at the current conductance parameters. Passed automatically by the optimizer.

S

Square, symmetric admissible genetic squared-distance matrix with zero diagonal. It must have the same dimensions as E and must correspond to a centered positive semidefinite covariance representation under the scaling used to construct it.

phi

Named numeric vector of nuisance parameters (tau, sigma). Omit to obtain default starting values c(1, 0).

nu

One finite positive number describing effective Wishart information. You must supply it; the fit does not estimate it. It is not the marker count. See the effective-information section and report sensitivity across plausible values with terradish_rescale_nu.

gradient

Logical. Compute gradient of the negative log-likelihood with respect to phi?

hessian

Logical. Compute Hessian with respect to phi?

partial

Logical. Compute second partial derivatives with respect to phi, E, and S?

nonnegative

Unused; present for interface consistency.

validate

Logical. Numerically validate gradients and Hessians via numDeriv? Very slow; for debugging small examples only.

Value

When phi is missing, a list with elements phi (starting values tau = 1 and sigma = 0), lower (c(0, -Inf)), and upper. Otherwise a list containing:

objective

Negative log-likelihood.

fitted

Matrix of expected squared genetic distances.

boundary

Logical; TRUE if tau = 0, indicating no detectable IBR signal.

gradient

Gradient with respect to phi (if gradient = TRUE).

hessian

Hessian matrix with respect to phi (if hessian = TRUE).

gradient_E

Gradient with respect to E (if partial = TRUE).

partial_E

Jacobian of gradient_E with respect to phi (if partial = TRUE).

partial_S

Jacobian of gradient with respect to the lower triangle of S (if partial = TRUE).

jacobian_E

Function for reverse-mode AD through E (if partial = TRUE).

jacobian_S

Function for reverse-mode AD through S (if partial = TRUE).

Details

The nuisance parameters are:

tau

Nonnegative scale applied to the conductance-implied covariance E. A tau near zero signals no detectable contribution from conductance-implied covariance under this model. This differs from tau in mlpe and leastsquares, where it is the log residual precision.

sigma

Log-scale identity component: the nugget variance added to the diagonal is \(\exp(\sigma)\). It represents diagonal variance not captured by the graph covariance, including sampling variation and model mismatch. It is not a smoothing scale or a direct estimate of genetic drift or population size. The simulators simulate_covariance_response and covariance_response_power take the nugget on its natural scale, so pass them exp() of a fitted sigma.

The fitted covariance is \(\Sigma = \tau E + \exp(\sigma) I\). The model evaluates the generalized Wishart log-likelihood for the observed admissible squared-distance matrix S after projecting out the grand mean, as described in McCullagh (2009).

generalized_wishart and wishart_covariance share the same \(\Sigma\) parameterization but differ in what S represents: this function takes a squared-distance matrix; wishart_covariance takes a covariance matrix. When the covariance and its implied distance representation carry the same information under the same centering, scaling, sites, and nu, the two functions return the same objective (up to numerical tolerance) because both use the same site-contrast likelihood and omit response-only normalizing terms. This equality does not make AIC values from arbitrary distance and covariance fits interchangeable.

\(F_{ST}\) ratio estimators do not have Wishart degrees of freedom. A passed geometry check is necessary but does not establish this sampling likelihood. Prefer covariance-derived squared distances and document the construction; use mlpe for ratio-estimator responses.

The function checks S with check_distance_response before evaluating the likelihood. Substantive violations stop the fit. Tiny structural deviations within the numerical tolerance are symmetrized and set to zero where appropriate. No Euclidean correction is applied.

Numerical nugget limits

Fitting uses the same small-nugget safeguards as wishart_covariance, retaining supplied bounds and fixed parameters. A verified numerical zero residual-variance limit is recorded separately from a zero graph contribution; summary() omits Wald uncertainty for its log-scale nugget coordinate.

Effective Wishart information

For Wishart likelihoods, nu scales the log likelihood. Point estimates do not depend on it, but standard errors, likelihood-ratio tests, and information criteria do. It is a dispersion parameter that you set, rather than the number of markers. Linkage and the population history shared by loci can make effective information much smaller than the SNP count. In unpublished forward-time simulations run during development, standard errors at the SNP count were three to five times smaller than the spread among replicate histories. Those model-based errors understated uncertainty.

Use terradish_cv_folds to compare conductance formulas, and terradish_rescale_nu to report inference across plausible values. For the same successful folds and nuisance settings, changing nu rescales Wishart CV scores without changing their ranking. Neither procedure identifies the true effective information or repairs an unsuitable response matrix.

References

McCullagh P. 2009. Marginal likelihood for distance matrices. Statistica Sinica 19:631-649.

See also

check_distance_response, wishart_covariance, wishart_covariates, mlpe, terradish

Other measurement models: leastsquares(), mlpe(), mlpe_covariates(), pairwise_covariates(), pairwise_endpoint_covariates(), terradish_measurement_model, wishart_covariance(), wishart_covariates()

Examples

library(terra)

data(melip)
covariates <- c(terra::unwrap(melip.altitude),
                terra::unwrap(melip.forestcover))
coords <- terra::unwrap(melip.coords)
names(covariates) <- c("altitude", "forestcover")
# Coarsened so the example runs quickly; name layers, then scale.
covariates <- scale_covariates(terra::aggregate(covariates, fact = 3,
                                                na.rm = TRUE))
# Keep one site per raster cell (some melip sites share a cell).
keep <- !duplicated(terra::cellFromXY(covariates, terra::crds(coords)))
coords <- coords[keep]
Fst <- melip.Fst[keep, keep]
surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords)

# Graph covariance (generalized inverse of the graph Laplacian) among the
# focal sites under uniform conductance (all coefficients zero).
laplacian_inv <- terradish_distance(theta = matrix(0, 1, 2),
                                    formula = ~ forestcover + altitude,
                                    data = surface,
                                    covariance = TRUE)$covariance[, , 1]

# Generate an admissible squared-distance response from a positive
# definite covariance, then evaluate the likelihood at known values.
set.seed(1)
Sigma <- 0.8 * laplacian_inv + 0.2 * diag(nrow(laplacian_inv))
observed_covariance <- rWishart(1, df = 40, Sigma = Sigma)[, , 1] / 40
observed_squared_distance <- dist_from_cov(observed_covariance)
check_distance_response(observed_squared_distance)$admissible
#> [1] TRUE
value <- generalized_wishart(laplacian_inv, observed_squared_distance,
                             nu = 40,
                             phi = c(tau = 0.8, sigma = log(0.2)))
value$objective  # negative log-likelihood; sigma is the LOG nugget
#> [1] -23.55683
